# A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement

Simon Leglaive    Xavier Alameda-Pineda ^(†)^(†)thanks: Xavier
Alameda-Pineda acknowledges the French National Research Agency (ANR)
for funding the ML3RI project. This work has been partially supported by
MIAI @ Grenoble Alpes, (ANR-19-P3IA-0003).    Laurent Girin    Radu
Horaud

###### Abstract

This paper presents a generative approach to speech enhancement based on
a recurrent variational autoencoder (RVAE). The deep generative speech
model is trained using clean speech signals only, and it is combined
with a nonnegative matrix factorization noise model for speech
enhancement. We propose a variational expectation-maximization algorithm
where the encoder of the RVAE is fine-tuned at test time, to approximate
the distribution of the latent variables given the noisy speech
observations. Compared with previous approaches based on feed-forward
fully-connected architectures, the proposed recurrent deep generative
speech model induces a posterior temporal dynamic over the latent
variables, which is shown to improve the speech enhancement results.

###### Index Terms: 

Speech enhancement, recurrent variational autoencoders, nonnegative
matrix factorization, variational inference.

^(†)^(†)address: ¹CentraleSupélec, IETR, France   ²Inria Grenoble
Rhône-Alpes, France  
  ³Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab, France

## 1 Introduction

Speech enhancement is an important problem in audio signal processing
\[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. The objective is to recover a clean speech signal
from a noisy mixture signal. In this work, we focus on single-channel
(i.e. single-microphone) speech enhancement.

Discriminative approaches based on deep neural networks have been
extensively used for speech enhancement. They try to estimate a clean
speech spectrogram or a time-frequency mask from a noisy speech
spectrogram, see e.g. \[[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4),
[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6)\]. Recently, deep generative speech
models based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] have
been investigated for single-channel \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9),
[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11)\] and multi-channel speech
enhancement \[[12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14)\]. A
pre-trained deep generative speech model is combined with a nonnegative
matrix factorization (NMF) \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] noise model whose
parameters are estimated at test time, from the observation of the noisy
mixture signal only. Compared with discriminative approaches, these
generative methods do not require pairs of clean and noisy speech signal
for training. This setting was referred to as “semi-supervised source
separation” in previous works \[[16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17),
[18](#bib.bib18)\], which should not be confused with the
supervised/unsupervised terminology of machine learning.

To the best of our knowledge, the aforementioned works on VAE-based deep
generative models for speech enhancement have only considered an
independent modeling of the speech time frames, through the use of
feed-forward and fully connected architectures. In this work, we propose
a recurrent VAE (RVAE) for modeling the speech signal. The generative
model is a special case of the one proposed in \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], but
the inference model for training is different. At test time, we develop
a variational expectation-maximization algorithm (VEM)
\[[20](#bib.bib20)\] to perform speech enhancement. The encoder of the
RVAE is fine-tuned to approximate the posterior distribution of the
latent variables, given the noisy speech observations. This model
induces a posterior temporal dynamic over the latent variables, which is
further propagated to the speech estimate. Experimental results show
that this approach outperforms its feed-forward and fully-connected
counterpart.

## 2 Deep generative speech model

### 2.1 Definition

Let $`\mathbf{s}=\{\mathbf{s}_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{F}\}_{n=0}^{N-1}`$
denote a sequence of short-time Fourier transform (STFT) speech time
frames, and
$`\mathbf{z}=\{\mathbf{z}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{L}\}_{n=0}^{N-1}`$ a
corresponding sequence of latent random vectors. We define the following
hierarchical generative speech model independently for all time frames
$`n\in\{0,...,N-1\}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{n}\mid\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_{c}\left(\mathbf{0},\diag\left\{\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})\right\}\right),\hskip 7.11317pt\text{with}\hskip 7.11317pt\mathbf{z}_{n}\overset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}\right),`$ |     | (1) |

and where $`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F}`$
will be defined by means of a _decoder_ neural network. $`\mathcal{N}`$
denotes the multivariate Gaussian distribution for a real-valued random
vector and $`\mathcal{N}_{c}`$ denotes the multivariate complex proper
Gaussian distribution \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]. Multiple choices are
possible to define the neural network corresponding to
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})`$, which will lead to different
probabilistic graphical models represented in
Fig. [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement").

#### FFNN generative speech model

$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec}}^{\text{FFNN}}(\mathbf{z}_{n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$
where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec}}^{\text{FFNN}}(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}):\mathbb{R}^{L}\mapsto\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F}`$
denotes a feed-forward fully-connected neural network (FFNN) of
parameters $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$. Such an architecture
was used in \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10),
[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13),
[14](#bib.bib14)\]. As represented in
Fig. [1a](#S2.F1.sf1 "In Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
this model results in the following factorization of the complete-data
likelihood:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}p(\mathbf{s}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})p(\mathbf{z}_{n}).
``` |  | (2) |

Note that in this case, the speech STFT time frames are not only
conditionally independent, but also marginally independent, i.e.
$`p(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}p(\mathbf{s}_{n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$.

#### RNN generative speech model

$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec},n}^{\text{RNN}}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$
where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec},n}^{\text{RNN}}(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}):\mathbb{R}^{L\times(n+1)}\mapsto\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F}`$
denotes the output at time frame $`n`$ of a recurrent neural network
(RNN), taking as input the sequence of latent random vectors
$`\mathbf{z}_{0:n}=\{\mathbf{z}_{n^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L}\}_{n^{\prime}=0}^{n}`$.
As represented in
Fig. [1b](#S2.F1.sf2 "In Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
we have the following factorization of the complete-data likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}p(\mathbf{s}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})p(\mathbf{z}_{n}).
``` |  | (3) |

Note that for this RNN-based model, the speech STFT time frames are
still conditionally independent, *but not marginally independent*.

#### BRNN generative speech model

$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec},n}^{\text{BRNN}}(\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$
where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{dec},n}^{\text{BRNN}}(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}):\mathbb{R}^{L\times N}\mapsto\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F}`$
denotes the output at time frame $`n`$ of a bidirectional RNN (BRNN)
taking as input the complete sequence of latent random vectors
$`\mathbf{z}`$. As represented in
Fig. [1c](#S2.F1.sf3 "In Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
we end up with the following factorization of the complete-data
likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}p(\mathbf{s}_{n}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})p(\mathbf{z}_{n}).
``` |  | (4) |

As for the RNN-based model, the speech STFT time frames are
conditionally independent but not marginally.

Note that for avoiding cluttered notations, the variance
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})`$ in the generative speech model
([1](#S2.E1 "In 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
is not made explicitly dependent on the decoder network parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$, but it clearly is.

### 2.2 Training

We would like to estimate the decoder parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$ in the maximum likelihood sense,
i.e. by maximizing
$`\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{I}\ln p\left(\mathbf{s}^{(i)};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}\right)`$,
where $`\{\mathbf{s}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{C}^{F\times N}\}_{i=1}^{I}`$ is a
training dataset consisting of $`I`$ i.i.d sequences of $`N`$ STFT
speech time frames. In the following, because it simplifies the
presentation, we simply omit the sum over the $`I`$ sequences and the
associated subscript $`(i)`$.

Due to the non-linear relationship between $`\mathbf{s}`$ and
$`\mathbf{z}`$, the marginal likelihood
$`p(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\int p(\mathbf{s}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})p(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z}`$
is analytically intractable, and it cannot be straightforwardly
optimized. We therefore resort to the framework of variational
autoencoders \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] for parameters estimation, which builds
upon stochastic fixed-form variational inference \[[22](#bib.bib22),
[23](#bib.bib23), [24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25),
[26](#bib.bib26)\].

This latter methodology first introduces a variational distribution
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ (or
inference model) parametrized by $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$,
which is an approximation of the true intractable posterior distribution
$`p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$. For any
variational distribution, we have the following decomposition of
log-marginal likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ln p(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{s}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})+D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\parallel p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})\big),
``` |  | (5) |

where
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{s}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$
is the *variational free energy* (VFE) (also referred to as the evidence
lower bound) defined by:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{s}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln p(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})-\ln q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hskip-42.67912pt=\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln p(\mathbf{s}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})\right]-D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\parallel p(\mathbf{z})\big),`$ |  | (6) |

and $`D_{\text{KL}}(q\parallel p)=\mathbb{E}_{q}[\ln q-\ln p]`$ is the
Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. As the latter is always non-negative,
we see from
([5](#S2.E5 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
that the VFE is a lower bound of the intractable log-marginal
likelihood. Moreover, we see that it is tight if and only if
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})=p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$.
Therefore, our objective is now to maximize the VFE with respect to
(w.r.t) both $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ and
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$. But in order to fully define the
VFE in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
we have to define the form of the variational distribution
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$.

Using the chain rule for joint distributions, the posterior distribution
of the latent vectors can be exactly expressed as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}p(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}),
``` |  | (7) |

where we considered
$`p(\mathbf{z}_{0}|\mathbf{z}_{-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=p(\mathbf{z}_{0}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})`$.
The variational distribution
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ is
naturally also expressed as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})=\prod\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}).
``` |  | (8) |

In this work,
$`q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$
denotes to the probability density function (pdf) of the following
Gaussian *inference model*:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s}),\diag\big\{\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\big\}\big),
``` |  | (9) |

where
$`\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n},\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}\}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{L}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{L}`$
will be defined by means of an *encoder* neural network.

#### Inference model for the BRNN generative speech model

For the BRNN generative speech model, the parameters of the variational
distribution in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
are defined by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n},\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}\}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{enc},n}^{\text{BRNN}}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}),`$ |  | (10) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{\text{enc},n}^{\text{BRNN}}(\cdot,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}):\mathbb{R}^{L\times n}\times\mathbb{C}^{F\times N}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{L}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{L}`$
denotes the output at time frame $`n`$ of a neural network whose
parameters are denoted by $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$. It is
composed of:

1.  1.
    *“Prediction block”*: a causal recurrent block processing
    $`\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1}`$;
2.  2.
    *“Observation block”*: a bidirectional recurrent block processing
    the complete sequence of STFT speech time frames $`\mathbf{s}`$;
3.  3.
    *“Update block”*: a feed-forward fully-connected block processing
    the outputs at time-frame $`n`$ of the two previous blocks.

If we want to sample from
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ in
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
we have to sample recursively each $`\mathbf{z}_{n}`$, starting from
$`n=0`$ up to $`N-1`$. Interestingly, the posterior is formed by running
*forward* over the latent vectors, and both *forward* and *backward*
over the input sequence of STFT speech time-frames. In other words, the
latent vector at a given time frame is inferred by taking into account
not only the latent vectors at the previous time steps, but also all the
speech STFT frames at the current, past and future time steps. The
anti-causal relationships were not taken into account in the RVAE model
\[[19](#bib.bib19)\].

#### Inference model for the RNN generative speech model

Using the fact that $`\mathbf{z}_{n}`$ is conditionally independent of
all other nodes in
Fig. [1b](#S2.F1.sf2 "In Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")
given its Markov blanket (defined as the set of parents, children and
co-parents of that node) \[[27](#bib.bib27)\],
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
can be simplified as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=p(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s}_{n:N-1};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}),
``` |  | (11) |

where
$`\mathbf{s}_{n:N-1}=\{\mathbf{s}_{n^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{C}^{F}\}_{n^{\prime}=n}^{N-1}`$.
This conditional independence also applies to the variational
distribution in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
whose parameters are now given by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n},\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}\}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\text{RNN}}_{\text{enc},n}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s}_{n:N-1};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}),`$ |  | (12) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\text{RNN}}_{\text{enc},n}(\cdot,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}):\mathbb{R}^{L\times n}\times\mathbb{C}^{F\times(N-n)}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{L}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{L}`$
denotes the same neural network as for the BRNN-based model, except that
the observation block is not a bidirectional recurrent block anymore,
but an *anti-causal* recurrent one. The full approximate posterior is
now formed by running *forward* over the latent vectors, and *backward*
over the input sequence of STFT speech time-frames.

#### Inference model for the FFNN generative speech model

For the same reason as before, by studying the Markov blanket of
$`\mathbf{z}_{n}`$ in
Fig. [1a](#S2.F1.sf1 "In Figure 1 ‣ BRNN generative speech model ‣ 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
the dependencies in
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
can be simplified as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})=p(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{s}_{n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}).
``` |  | (13) |

This simplification also applies to the variational distribution in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
whose parameters are now given by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n},\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}\}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})=\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\text{FFNN}}_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{s}_{n};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}),
``` |  | (14) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\text{FFNN}}_{\text{enc}}(\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}):\mathbb{C}^{F}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{L}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{L}`$
denotes the output of an FFNN. Such an architecture was used in
\[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11),
[12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14)\]. This is the only
case where, from the approximate posterior, we can sample all latent
vectors in parallel for all time frames, without further approximation.

Here also, the mean and variance vectors in the inference model
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
are not made explicitly dependent on the encoder network parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$, but they clearly are.

#### Variational free energy

Given the generative model
([1](#S2.E1 "In 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
and the general inference model
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
we can develop the VFE defined in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
as follows (derivation details are provided in
Appendix [A.1](#S1.SS1 "A.1 Variational free energy derivation details ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{s}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})\overset{c}{=}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\sum\limits_{f=0}^{F-1}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\Big[d_{\text{IS}}\left(|s_{fn}|^{2},v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})\right)\Big]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt+\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{l=0}^{L-1}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\Big[\ln\big(v_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\big)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\qquad-\mu_{\mathbf{z},ln}^{2}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})-v_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\Big],`$ |  | (15) |

where $`\overset{c}{=}`$ denotes equality up to an additive constant
w.r.t $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ and
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$,
$`d_{\text{IS}}(a,b)=a/b-\ln(a/b)-1`$ is the Itakura-Saito (IS)
divergence \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], $`s_{fn}\in\mathbb{C}`$ and
$`v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}`$ denote respectively
the $`f`$-th entries of $`\mathbf{s}_{n}`$ and
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})`$, and
$`\mu_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\in\mathbb{R}`$ and
$`v_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}`$
denote respectively the $`l`$-th entry of
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})`$ and
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})`$.

The expectations in
([15](#S2.E15 "In Variational free energy ‣ 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
are analytically intractable, so we compute unbiased Monte Carlo
estimates using a set $`\{\mathbf{z}^{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{R}`$ of i.i.d.
realizations drawn from
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$. For that
purpose, we use the “reparametrization trick” introduced in
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. The obtained objective function is differentiable
w.r.t to both $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$ and
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$, and it can be optimized using
gradient-ascent-based algorithms. Finally, we recall that in the final
expression of the VFE, there should actually be an additional sum over
the $`I`$ i.i.d. sequences in the training dataset
$`\{\mathbf{s}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{I}`$. For stochastic or mini-batch
optimization algorithms, we would only consider a subset of these
training sequences for each update of the model parameters.

## 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm

### 3.1 Speech, noise and mixture model

The deep generative *clean* speech model along with its parameters
learning procedure were defined in the previous section. For speech
enhancement, we now consider a Gaussian noise model based on an NMF
parametrization of the variance \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. Independently for
all time frames $`n\in\{0,...,N-1\}`$, we have:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{b}_{n}\sim\mathcal{N}_{c}(\mathbf{0},\diag\{\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{b},n}\}),
``` |  | (16) |

where $`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{b},n}=(\mathbf{W}_{b}\mathbf{H}_{b})_{:,n}`$
with $`\mathbf{W}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F\times K}`$ and
$`\mathbf{H}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K\times N}`$.

The noisy mixture signal is modeled as
$`\mathbf{x}_{n}=\sqrt{g_{n}}\mathbf{s}_{n}+\mathbf{b}_{n}`$, where
$`g_{n}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}`$ is a gain parameter scaling the level of the
speech signal at each time frame \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. We further consider
the independence of the speech and noise signals so that the likelihood
is defined by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{x}_{n}\mid\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_{c}\left(\mathbf{0},\diag\{\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{x},n}(\mathbf{z})\}\right),
``` |  | (17) |

where
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{x},n}(\mathbf{z})=g_{n}\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s},n}(\mathbf{z})+\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{b},n}`$.

### 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm

We consider that the speech model parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$ which have been learned during the
training stage are fixed, so we omit them in the rest of this section.
We now need to estimate the remaining model parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\phi}=\left\{\mathbf{g}=[g_{0},...,g_{N-1}]^{\top},\mathbf{W}_{b},\mathbf{H}_{b}\right\}`$
from the observation of the noisy mixture signal
$`\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{F}\}_{n=0}^{N-1}`$. However,
very similarly as for the training stage (see
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
the marginal likelihood $`p(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})`$ is
intractable, and we resort again to variational inference. The VFE at
test time is defined by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\phi})\hskip-0.85355pt=\hskip-0.85355pt\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\hskip-0.85355pt\left[\hskip-0.85355pt\ln p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\phi})\hskip-0.85355pt\right]-D_{\text{KL}}\big(\hskip-0.85355ptq(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\parallel p(\mathbf{z})\hskip-1.42271pt\big).
``` |  | (18) |

Following a VEM algorithm \[[20](#bib.bib20)\], we will maximize this
criterion alternatively w.r.t $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ at
the E-step, and $`\boldsymbol{\phi}`$ at the M-step. Note that here
also, we have
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\phi})\leq\ln p(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})`$
with equality if and only if
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})=p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})`$.

#### Variational E-Step with fine-tuned encoder

We consider a fixed-form variational inference strategy, reusing the
inference model learned during the training stage. More precisely, the
variational distribution
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ is defined
exactly as $`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$
in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
and
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
except that $`\mathbf{s}`$ is replaced with $`\mathbf{x}`$. Remember
that the mean and variance vectors
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\cdot,\cdot)`$ and
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{z},n}(\cdot,\cdot)`$ in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
correspond to the VAE encoder network, whose parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ were estimated along with the
parameters $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$ of the generative speech
model. During the training stage, this encoder network took *clean
speech* signals as input. It is now *fine-tuned* with a *noisy speech*
signal as input. For that purpose, we maximize
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\phi})`$
w.r.t $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ only, with fixed
$`\boldsymbol{\phi}`$. This criterion takes the exact same form as
([15](#S2.E15 "In Variational free energy ‣ 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
except that $`|s_{fn}|^{2}`$ is replaced with $`|x_{fn}|^{2}`$ where
$`x_{fn}\in\mathbb{C}`$ denotes the $`f`$-th entry of
$`\mathbf{x}_{n}`$, $`\mathbf{s}`$ is replaced with $`\mathbf{x}`$, and
$`v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})`$ is replaced with
$`v_{\mathbf{x},fn}(\mathbf{z})`$, the $`f`$-th entry of
$`\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{x},n}(\mathbf{z})`$ which was defined along with
([17](#S3.E17 "In 3.1 Speech, noise and mixture model ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).
Exactly as in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
intractable expectations are replaced with a Monte Carlo estimate and
the VFE is maximized w.r.t. $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ by
means of gradient-based optimization techniques. In summary, we use the
framework of VAEs \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] both at training for estimating
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$ and
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ from clean speech signals, and at
testing for fine-tuning $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ from the
noisy speech signal, and with $`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}}`$
fixed. The idea of refitting the encoder was also proposed in
\[[28](#bib.bib28)\] in a different context.

#### Point-estimate E-Step

In the experiments, we will compare this variational E-step with an
alternative proposed in \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], which consists in relying
only on a point estimate of the latent variables. In our framework, this
approach can be understood as assuming that the approximate posterior
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ is a dirac
delta function centered at the maximum a posteriori estimate
$`\mathbf{z}^{\star}`$. Maximization of
$`p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})\propto p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\phi})p(\mathbf{z})`$
w.r.t $`\mathbf{z}`$ can be achieved by means of gradient-based
techniques, where backpropagation is used to compute the gradient w.r.t.
the input of the generative decoder network.

#### M-Step

For both the VEM algorithm and the point-estimate alternative, the
M-Step consists in maximizing
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}},\boldsymbol{\phi})`$
w.r.t. $`\boldsymbol{\phi}`$ under a non-negativity constraint and with
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$ fixed. Replacing intractable
expectations with Monte Carlo estimates, the M-step can be recast as
minimizing the following criterion \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\phi})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum\nolimits_{r=1}^{R}\sum\nolimits_{f=0}^{F-1}\sum\nolimits_{n=0}^{N-1}d_{\text{IS}}\left(|x_{fn}|^{2},v_{\mathbf{x},fn}\left(\mathbf{z}^{(r)}\right)\right),`$ |  | (19) |

where $`v_{\mathbf{x},fn}(\mathbf{z}^{(r)})`$ implicitly depends on
$`\boldsymbol{\phi}`$. For the VEM algorithm,
$`\{\mathbf{z}^{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{R}`$ is a set of i.i.d. sequences drawn
from $`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ using
the current value of the parameters
$`\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}}`$. For the point estimate approach,
$`R=1`$ and $`\mathbf{z}^{(1)}`$ corresponds to the maximum a posteriori
estimate. This optimization problem can be tackled using a
majorize-minimize approach \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], which leads to the
multiplicative update rules derived in \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] using the
methodology proposed in \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] (these updates are recalled
in
Appendix [A.2](#S1.SS2 "A.2 Update rules for the M-step ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).

#### Speech reconstruction

Given the estimated model parameters, we want to compute the posterior
mean of the speech coefficients:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{s}_{fn}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(s_{fn}\mid x_{fn};\boldsymbol{\phi})}[s_{fn}]=\mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})}\left[\frac{\sqrt{g_{n}}v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})}{v_{\mathbf{x},fn}(\mathbf{z})}\right]x_{fn}.`$ |  | (20) |

In practice, the speech estimate is actually given by the scaled
coefficients $`\sqrt{g_{n}}\hat{s}_{fn}`$. Note that
([20](#S3.E20 "In Speech reconstruction ‣ 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
corresponds to a Wiener-like filtering, averaged over all possible
realizations of the latent variables according to their posterior
distribution. As before, this expectation is intractable, but we
approximate it by a Monte Carlo estimate using samples drawn from
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ for the
VEM algorithm. For the point-estimate approach,
$`p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\phi})`$ is approximated by a
dirac delta function centered at the maximum a posteriori.

In the case of the RNN- and BRNN-based generative speech models (see
Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
it is important to remember that sampling from
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ is
actually done recursively, by sampling
$`q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$
from $`n=0`$ to $`N-1`$ (see
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).
Therefore, there is a *posterior temporal dynamic* that will be
propagated from the latent vectors to the estimated speech signal,
through the expectation in the Wiener-like filtering of
([20](#S3.E20 "In Speech reconstruction ‣ 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).
This temporal dynamic is expected to be beneficial compared with the
FFNN generative speech model, where the speech estimate is built
independently for all time frames.

## 4 Experiments

#### Dataset

The deep generative speech models are trained using around 25 hours of
clean speech data, from the "si_tr_s" subset of the Wall Street Journal
(WSJ0) dataset \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]. Early stopping with a patience of
20 epochs is performed using the subset "si_dt_05" (around 2 hours of
speech). We removed the trailing and leading silences for each
utterance. For testing, we used around 1.5 hours of noisy speech,
corresponding to 651 synthetic mixtures. The clean speech signals are
taken from the "si_et_05" subset of WSJ0 (unseen speakers), and the
noise signals from the "verification" subset of the QUT-NOISE dataset
\[[33](#bib.bib33)\]. Each mixture is created by uniformly sampling a
noise type among {"café", "home", "street", "car"} and a signal-to-noise
ratio (SNR) among {-5, 0, 5} dB. The intensity of each signal for
creating a mixture at a given SNR is computed using the ITU-R BS.1770-4
protocol \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. Note that an SNR computed with this
protocol is here 2.5 dB *lower* (in average) than with a simple sum of
the squared signal coefficients. Finally, all signals have a
16 kHz-sampling rate, and the STFT is computed using a 64-ms sine window
(i.e. $`F=513`$) with 75%-overlap.

#### Network architecture and training parameters

All details regarding the encoder and decoder network architectures and
their training procedure are provided in
Appendix [A.3](#S1.SS3 "A.3 Neural network architectures and training ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement").

#### Speech enhancement parameters

The dimension of the latent space for the deep generative speech model
is fixed to $`L=16`$. The rank of the NMF-based noise model is fixed to
$`K=8`$. $`\mathbf{W}_{b}`$ and $`\mathbf{H}_{b}`$ are randomly
initialized (with a fixed seed to ensure fair comparisons), and
$`\mathbf{g}`$ is initialized with an all-ones vector. For computing
([19](#S3.E19 "In M-Step ‣ 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")),
we fix the number of samples to $`R=1`$, which is also the case for
building the Monte Carlo estimate of
([20](#S3.E20 "In Speech reconstruction ‣ 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).
The VEM algorithm and its "point estimate" alternative (referred to as
PEEM) are run for 500 iterations. We used Adam \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] with
a step size of $`10^{-2}`$ for the gradient-based iterative optimization
technique involved at the E-step. For the FFNN deep generative speech
model, it was found that an insufficient number of gradient steps had a
strong negative impact on the results, so it was fixed to 10. For the
(B)RNN model, this choice had a much lesser impact so it was fixed to 1,
thus limiting the computational burden.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Algorithm | Model | SI-SDR (dB) | PESQ | ESTOI |
| MCEM \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] | FFNN | 5.4 $`\pm`$ 0.4 | 2.22 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.60 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
| PEEM | FFNN | 4.4 $`\pm`$ 0.4 | 2.21 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.58 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
|  | RNN | 5.8 $`\pm`$ 0.5 | 2.33 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.63 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
|  | BRNN | 5.4 $`\pm`$ 0.5 | 2.30 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.62 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
| VEM | FFNN | 4.4 $`\pm`$ 0.4 | 1.93 $`\pm`$ 0.05 | 0.53 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
|  | RNN | 6.8 $`\pm`$ 0.4 | 2.33 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.67 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
|  | BRNN | 6.9 $`\pm`$ 0.5 | 2.35 $`\pm`$ 0.04 | 0.67 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
| noisy mixture |  | -2.6 $`\pm`$ 0.5 | 1.82 $`\pm`$ 0.03 | 0.49 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |
| oracle Wiener filtering |  | 12.1 $`\pm`$ 0.3 | 3.13 $`\pm`$ 0.02 | 0.88 $`\pm`$ 0.01 |

Table 1: Median results and confidence intervals.

#### Results

We compare the performance of the VEM and PEEM algorithms for the three
types of deep generative speech model. For the FFNN model only, we also
compare with the Monte Carlo EM (MCEM) algorithm proposed in
\[[9](#bib.bib9)\] (which cannot be straightforwardly adapted to the
(B)RNN model). The enhanced speech quality is evaluated in terms of
scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) in dB
\[[36](#bib.bib36)\], perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ)
measure (between -0.5 and 4.5) \[[37](#bib.bib37)\] and extended
short-time objective intelligibility (ESTOI) measure (between 0 and 1)
\[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. For all measures, the higher the better. The
median results for all SNRs along with their confidence interval are
presented in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Speech enhancement parameters ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement").
Best results are in black-color-bold font, while gray-color-bold font
indicates results that are not significantly different. As a reference,
we also provide the results obtained with the noisy mixture signal as
the speech estimate, and with oracle Wiener filtering. Note that oracle
results are here particularly low, which shows the difficulty of the
dataset. Oracle SI-SDR is for instance 7 dB lower than the one in
\[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. Therefore, the VEM and PEEM results should not be
directly compared with the MCEM results provided in \[[9](#bib.bib9)\],
but only with the ones provided here.

From
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Speech enhancement parameters ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"),
we can draw the following conclusions: First, we observe that for the
FFNN model, the VEM algorithm performs poorly. In this setting, the
performance measures actually strongly decrease after the first
50-to-100 iterations of the algorithm. We did not observe this behavior
for the (B)RNN model. We argue that the posterior temporal dynamic over
the latent variables helps the VEM algorithm finding a satisfactory
estimate of the overparametrized posterior model
$`q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$. Second,
the superiority of the RNN model over the FFNN one is confirmed for all
algorithms in this comparison. However, the bidirectional model (BRNN)
does not perform significantly better than the unidirectional one.
Third, the VEM algorithm outperforms the PEEM one, which shows the
interest of using the full (approximate) posterior distribution of the
latent variables and not only the maximum-a-posteriori point estimate
for estimating the noise and mixture model parameters. Audio examples
and code are available online \[[39](#bib.bib39)\].

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we proposed a recurrent deep generative speech model and a
variational EM algorithm for speech enhancement. We showed that
introducing a temporal dynamic is clearly beneficial in terms of speech
enhancement. Future works include developing a Markov chain EM algorithm
to measure the quality of the proposed variational approximation of the
intractable true posterior distribution.

## A Appendix

### A.1 Variational free energy derivation details

In this section we give derivation details for obtaining the expression
of the variational free energy in
([15](#S2.E15 "In Variational free energy ‣ 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).
We will develop the two terms involved in the definition of the
variational free energy in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).

#### Data-fidelity term

From the generative model defined in
([1](#S2.E1 "In 2.1 Definition ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
we have:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}`$ | $`\displaystyle\left[\ln p(\mathbf{s}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln p(\mathbf{s}_{n}|\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{dec}})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle-\sum_{f=0}^{F-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln\big(v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})\big)+\frac{|s_{fn}|^{2}}{v_{\mathbf{s},fn}(\mathbf{z})}\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-FN\ln(\pi)`$ |  | (21) |

#### Regularization term

From the inference model defined in
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
and
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
we have:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\big(q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\parallel p(\mathbf{z})\big)`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})-\ln p(\mathbf{z})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})-\ln p(\mathbf{z}_{n})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{0:n}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[\ln q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})-\ln p(\mathbf{z}_{n})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\big[\ln q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt-\ln p(\mathbf{z}_{n})\big]\Big]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\Big(q(\mathbf{z}_{n}|\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})\parallel p(\mathbf{z}_{n})\Big)\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=\,`$ | $`\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1}|\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{enc}})}\Big[\ln\big(v_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\big)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt-\mu_{\mathbf{z},ln}^{2}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})-v_{\mathbf{z},ln}(\mathbf{z}_{0:n-1},\mathbf{s})\Big]-\frac{NL}{2}.`$ |  | (22) |

Summing up
([21](#S1.E21 "In Data-fidelity term ‣ A.1 Variational free energy derivation details ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
and
([22](#S1.E22 "In Regularization term ‣ A.1 Variational free energy derivation details ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
and recognizing the IS divergence we end up with the expression of the
variational free energy in
([15](#S2.E15 "In Variational free energy ‣ 2.2 Training ‣ 2 Deep generative speech model ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")).

### A.2 Update rules for the M-step

The multiplicative update rules for minimizing
([19](#S3.E19 "In M-Step ‣ 3.2 Speech enhancement algorithm ‣ 3 Speech enhancement: Model and algorithm ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement"))
using a majorize-minimize technique \[[30](#bib.bib30),
[31](#bib.bib31)\] are given by (see \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] for derivation
details):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{H}_{b}\leftarrow\mathbf{H}_{b}\odot\left[\frac{\mathbf{W}_{b}^{\top}\left(\mid\mathbf{X}\mid^{\odot 2}\odot\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-2}\right)}{\mathbf{W}_{b}^{\top}\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-1}}\right]^{\odot 1/2};
``` |  | (23) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{W}_{b}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{b}\odot\left[\frac{\left(\mid\mathbf{X}\mid^{\odot 2}\odot\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-2}\right)\mathbf{H}_{b}^{\top}}{\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-1}\mathbf{H}_{b}^{\top}}\right]^{\odot 1/2};
``` |  | (24) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{g}^{\top}\leftarrow\mathbf{g}^{\top}\odot\left[\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\left[\mid\mathbf{X}\mid^{\odot 2}\odot\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)}\odot\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-2}\right)\right]}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\left[\sum\limits_{r=1}^{R}\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)}\odot\left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\right)^{\odot-1}\right)\right]}\right]^{\odot 1/2},
``` |  | (25) |

where $`\odot`$ denotes element-wise multiplication and exponentiation,
matrix division is also element-wise,
$`\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{x}}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{F\times N}`$
are the matrices of entries
$`v_{\mathbf{s},fn}\left(\mathbf{z}^{(r)}\right)`$ and
$`v_{\mathbf{x},fn}\left(\mathbf{z}^{(r)}\right)`$ respectively,
$`\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{F\times N}`$ is the matrix of entries
$`x_{fn}`$ and $`\mathbf{1}`$ is an all-ones column vector of dimension
$`F`$. Note that non-negativity of $`\mathbf{H}_{b}`$,
$`\mathbf{W}_{b}`$ and $`\mathbf{g}`$ is ensured provided that they are
initialized with non-negative values.

Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ A.3 Neural network architectures and training ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement").

The decoder and encoder network architectures are represented in
Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ A.3 Neural network architectures and training ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")
and
Fig. [3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ A.3 Neural network architectures and training ‣ A Appendix ‣ A Recurrent Variational Autoencoder for Speech Enhancement")
respectively. The "dense" (i.e. feed-forward fully-connected) output
layers are of dimension $`L=16`$ and $`F=513`$ for the encoder and
decoder, respectively. The dimension of all other layers was arbitrarily
fixed to 128. RNN layers correspond to long short-term memory (LSTM)
ones \[[40](#bib.bib40)\]. For the FFNN generative model, a batch is
made of 128 time frames of clean speech power spectrogram. For the
(B)RNN generative model, a batch is made 32 sequences of 50 time frames.
Given an input sequence, all LSTM hidden states for the encoder and
decoder networks are initialized to zero. For training, we use the Adam
optimizer \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] with a step size of $`10^{-3}`$,
exponential decay rates of $`0.9`$ and $`0.999`$ for the first and
second moment estimates, respectively, and an epsilon of $`10^{-8}`$ for
preventing division by zero.
````
